Selected Chemical Composition Values by Weight Element 6061 Aluminum 7075 Aluminum Aluminum (Al) ~97.9% (balance) ~90.0% (balance) Zinc (Zn) — 5.6% Magnesium (Mg) 1.0% 2.5% Copper (Cu) 0.28% 1.6% Silicon (Si) 0.6% — Chromium (Cr) 0.20% 0.23% 6061 develops strength primarily through Mg-Si precipitates after solution heat treatment and aging, while 7075 is a high-strength Al-Zn-Mg-Cu alloy. The lower corrosion and stress-corrosion-cracking resistance of 7075-T6/T651 in certain environments results from the combined effects of alloy chemistry, temper, microstructure, grain orientation, sustained stress, and exposure conditions. It should not be attributed to copper content alone. 7075 vs 6061 Aluminum Temper and Stock Form: Why They Matter T6 temper involves solution heat treatment, quenching, and artificial aging. T651 adds stress relief by stretching after quenching and before artificial aging. This reduces residual stress in the stock and helps limit distortion during machining, although it does not eliminate the risk of movement when large amounts of material are removed. Billet form is worth a sentence as well. Flat pocketed parts start from plate, and turned parts from bar stock, while deep housings need block, which brings the removal-volume problem with it, because most of a block ends up as chips and 7075 chips cost real money even after the scrap credit. 6061 vs 7075: Strength and Mechanical Performance Tensile Strength and Yield Strength Yield strength is the number to design against for a machined bracket, because once the stress passes yield, the part stays bent even though fracture happens at a considerably higher stress. Tensile matters for ultimate failures, but on shop parts the permanent set arrives first. The gap between the two alloys is large. 6061-T6 yields between 240 and 276 MPa depending on product form, while 7075-T6 starts at 455 and reaches 503, so a bracket that must survive a high load inside a tight envelope can drop its wall thickness considerably in 7075 and still stay under yield. An enclosure cover carrying almost nothing cannot use the extra strength at all, and hole or thread stress concentrations will eat the margin in either alloy when the detail design is poor. Elastic Modulus 7075 is slightly stiffer than 6061, so a part of the same geometry may deflect slightly less under the same load. Geometry usually has a greater effect. For example, doubling the section depth of a rectangular cantilever in the bending direction reduces elastic deflection to one eighth when the load, span, width, and material stay the same. For a stiffness-limited design, check the section geometry and support spacing before changing alloys. Fatigue Strength for Cyclic and Repeated Loads Fatigue is where the alloys split hardest. Rotating-beam tests at 5×10⁸ cycles put 6061-T6 near 96 MPa and 7075-T6 near 159 MPa, which is why links and anything bolted to a vibrating assembly usually end up in 7075. Those numbers come with conditions attached, because fatigue results scatter badly with surface finish and with grain direction, so a real design should use data matched to its own geometry rather than a table value. Machined surfaces deserve a specific mention here: tool marks act as crack initiation sites, so on a fatigue-critical face the finishing pass contributes to the strength result. Density and Strength-to-Weight Ratio 7075 is 4% denser, 2.81 against 2.70 g/cm³. Against a strength advantage near 80%, the density penalty only matters in designs where the section cannot be thinned, and those are usually the stiffness-limited designs where 7075 was the wrong choice anyway. Where thinning is possible, specific strength dominates and 7075 wins. 7075 vs 6061 for CNC Machining For most CNC-machined aluminum parts , 6061-T6 is the more economical starting point, while 7075-T6 is worth considering when the design requires higher yield strength without a major increase in part weight. Cutting Performance and Tool Wear On the machine, the difference shows up in the chips before anywhere else. 6061-T6 curls into long strings and tends to weld itself onto the cutting edge at conservative speeds, which sharp polished carbide and generous lubrication keep under control, while 7075-T6 breaks into short C-shaped chips, gives a better as-machined surface, and pushes cutting forces and flank wear up at the same time. The net effect on cost between the two is small and part-specific. Both alloys run happily on carbide at 300 to 600 m/min surface speed on a modern VMC. Machining Distortion and Dimensional Stability Residual stress in the stock is the hidden cost of cutting. When a deep pocket goes into one face of 40 mm plate and the opposite face stays solid, the remaining material rebalances and the part bows, and pocketed plates machined in a single pass commonly move a few tenths of a millimeter before anyone touches a straightedge. T651 plate, stretched at the mill, drops that risk a long way without eliminating it. Sequencing handles the rest. Rough everything first and leave 0.3 to 0.5 mm of stock; a rest period or a stress-relief cycle before the finishing cuts then keeps critical faces close to where the program put them. Support tabs left on thin sections until the late operations help as well. Thin Walls, Surface Finish, and Tolerances Thin walls deflect under cutting force and spring back once the tool clears, in either alloy, since their elastic moduli are similar. Wall thickness and unsupported span determine the extent of deflection, while tool engagement affects the final dimensional accuracy. JLCCNC can machine metal walls as thin as 0.8 mm and plastic walls as thin as 1.5 mm. For these features, temporary ribs or tabbed stock can provide additional support and help control deformation during machining. JLCCNC applies ISO 2768-m as its default general machining tolerance. A tolerance of ±0.02 mm can be specified for individual features on the drawing, subject to a feasibility review before production. Thermal expansion also matters during inspection: both alloys have a coefficient of thermal expansion of approximately 23.5 μm/(m·K). A 100 mm part changes in length by about 23.5 μm over a 10 °C temperature difference. Parts should be allowed to stabilize at the inspection temperature before critical dimensions are measured. Welding and Joining: 6061 vs 7075 6061 is a weldable alloy. Standard TIG or MIG welding with ER4043 or ER5356 filler can produce sound 6061 joints. However, the heat-affected zone loses a substantial amount of its T6 strength due to overaging. Its post-weld strength depends on the welding procedure and any subsequent heat treatment, which can also introduce distortion into the assembly. Conventional fusion welding is generally not recommended for 7075 because its alloy composition makes the fusion zone highly susceptible to hot cracking. Mechanical fasteners and adhesive bonding are more practical joining methods for most machined 7075 parts. Friction stir welding is a specialized solid-state process used in some industrial and aerospace applications. The design consequence follows directly from that constraint. A simple assembly of plates and profiles is often cheaper as welded 6061, accepting the weld distortion and the softened HAZ, while a component whose loads justify 7075 usually gets machined from billet in one piece, which keeps full parent strength and holds tight feature-to-feature relationships at the cost of chip volume and cycle time. Between these two alloys, 6061 is generally the better starting point for conventional fusion welding. Evaluate the joint strength using the as-welded condition or the specified post-weld treatment. Is 6061 or 7075 More Cost-Effective to Machine? Between the two alloys, the machining cost itself barely moves, since cycle time and removal volume set the quote, with setup count close behind. 7075 wears tools somewhat faster in deep features and cuts slightly slower, against which its clean chip breaking saves finishing time, and on balance the difference is small enough to decide part by part. 6061 vs 7075: Corrosion Resistance and Anodizing Corrosion Resistance in Different Environments 6061 generally offers better corrosion resistance than 7075 and is often the better starting point for parts exposed to saltwater or de-icing salts. In chloride environments, 7075-T6 and 7075-T651 can develop stress corrosion cracking under sustained tensile stress. Overaged tempers such as 7075-T73 and 7075-T7351 can improve resistance to stress corrosion cracking at the cost of some strength. Neither alloy should be chosen for chemical service from a rating table, because compatibility depends on concentration and temperature as much as on the medium itself. Anodizing 6061 vs 7075 Both alloys anodize, and Type II decorative coatings and Type III hard coats both work. What differs is appearance, since 6061 takes a clear, consistent film that dyes evenly across batches, while 7075's alloying elements tint the oxide gray-yellow and shift between lots, which makes color matching on mixed batches difficult. Type III hard anodizing on 7075, typically 25 to 80 μm, is the usual treatment where wear resistance matters. Anodizing changes the final dimensions of a part. As a general estimate, about half of the coating thickness may build outward from the original surface. A 15 μm Type II coating can therefore add roughly 7.5 μm to each coated surface, which may affect a close-fitting assembly or threaded feature. Specify any threads or precision mating surfaces that require protection from coating buildup, and confirm masking feasibility before production. A finish sample is also useful when color consistency is critical. What Are 6061 and 7075 Aluminum Used For? Applications of 6061 Aluminum Typical 6061 work passing through the shop includes equipment housings, mounting brackets, frames, and heat sinks. For heat sinks the 167 W/(m·K) conductivity does the work, and 6061 also carries a higher long-term service temperature, around 150 °C, before overaging becomes an issue, while 7075-T6 starts losing strength above roughly 120 °C given time. Welded assemblies and outdoor hardware round out the list, and a standard case is a machined enclosure with tapped holes and internal pockets at moderate load, anodized, delivered in 6061-T6. Applications of 7075 Aluminum Most of the 7075 we quote is high-load brackets and links in cycling service, plus one-piece parts that replace welded assemblies where a smaller section is worth the material premium. A drone arm is the standard example, with a small section carrying real loads while every gram is counted. Calling the alloy aerospace-grade describes the material rather than the part. Flight-qualified hardware requires material certification and traceability, which ordering 7075 stock does not provide. 7075 vs 6061: Cost Comparison Raw Material Cost 6061 stock typically prices 20 to 30% under 7075, with the exact gap depending on form and lot size. Availability matters at least as much day to day, since 6061 is stocked in the widest range of sizes and ships fastest, while 7075 covers common dimensions off the shelf and odd sizes can require custom sourcing, so it is worth confirming availability before the design freezes rather than after. Total CNC Part Cost A part price is not the alloy price multiplied by weight. Removal volume comes first, because machining an 8 kg housing out of a 70 kg block means paying for 62 kg of material in order to haul it away as chips, and at 7075 pricing that line item dominates the quote. Cycle time across the setups follows, and inspection load behind it wherever the tolerance scheme is tight. On small parts the alloy premium barely registers. Both alloys are fully recyclable and chips carry credit against the job, which softens the arithmetic without changing it. Whether 7075 pays is a design question with two honest answers. If the part fails, or shrinks meaningfully, because of the higher strength, the premium earns itself back, and if 6061 clears the stress check with margin, the premium buys nothing. The premium also lands unevenly on the quote, which is worth spelling out: on a part where stock accounts for 30% of the price, a 25% alloy premium moves the total by under 8%, while on heavy-removal work where the billet dominates the quote, the same premium moves it several times that. For a specific part, the material cost difference is easier to judge from the actual design. Upload your CAD files to get an instant CNC machining quote and DFM feedback from JLCCNC engineers. How to Choose Between 6061 and 7075 for CNC Parts The selection runs in a fixed order on our side. Loads and allowable stress come first, then a decision on whether strength or stiffness governs the design, remembering that stiffness answers to geometry rather than to alloy. Corrosion exposure and finish requirements come next, and cost comes last, compared on total part cost rather than per kilogram. A drawing whose worst stress sits comfortably under 6061's yield does not improve in 7075. Drawings with thin walls and deep cavities, especially with tight positional tolerances on top of either, should come to us before release, since we review manufacturability and quote both alloys so the choice gets made on numbers instead of on property tables. Design requirement More suitable starting point Reason General-purpose CNC parts 6061-T6 Balanced properties and cost High yield-strength requirement 7075-T6 Greater resistance to permanent deformation Cyclic / repeated loading 7075-T6 ~60% higher fatigue strength Welded structure 6061 Conventional weldability One-piece high-load component 7075 Machined from billet replaces weldments Corrosive or marine environment 6061 Better corrosion resistance, lower SCC risk Decorative anodized finish 6061 Consistent appearance Heat-dissipating component 6061 Higher thermal conductivity, higher service temperature High strength-to-weight ratio 7075-T6 Much higher strength, ~4% denser Large plate-machined part, distortion-sensitive 6061-T651 or 7075-T651 Stress-relieved plate helps reduce residual-stress-related distortion Cost-sensitive component 6061 Lower material cost Precision CNC Machining Service Comparing 6061 and 7075 for a machined part? Upload your CAD files to get an instant CNC machining quote and DFM feedback from JLCCNC engineers. Get Instant Quote FAQs About 7075 and 6061 Aluminum Is 7075 aluminum stronger than 6061? Yes. 7075-T6 generally has higher tensile and yield strength than 6061-T6. The exact difference depends on the product form, thickness, and specification. Can 7075 aluminum be welded? Not by conventional fusion welding. Hot cracking in the Zn-Cu chemistry makes the joint unreliable, and the heat-affected zone loses the temper regardless. Bolted or bonded joints, or machining the part in one piece, are the workarounds. Designs that must be welded should specify 6061. Is 6061 or 7075 better for CNC machining? Both cut well. 6061 strings and builds up on edges at low speed, while 7075 breaks chips cleanly and finishes better but wears tools faster. The choice should follow the part's requirements rather than how either alloy machines. Can 6061 and 7075 aluminum both be anodized? Yes, both Type II and Type III. 6061 takes a clear, consistent film; 7075 anodizes gray-yellow with lot-to-lot variation. Cosmetic parts are safer in 6061. Does 7075 aluminum corrode faster than 6061? 7075 aluminum is generally more susceptible to corrosion than 6061, particularly in chloride environments. The risk of pitting and stress corrosion cracking depends on the alloy temper, sustained tensile stress, and exposure conditions. For marine applications, 6061 is generally the more suitable choice. If 7075 is required, a T73 temper can improve stress corrosion cracking resistance, while a protective coating provides additional corrosion protection. Is 6061 aluminum cheaper than 7075? As raw stock, typically 20 to 30% cheaper. The finished part price depends more on removal volume and cycle time than on the alloy. Is 7075 aluminum worth the extra cost? It earns the premium when the load case or the weight budget makes the strength necessary, and the part usually shrinks as a result, paying some of it back. When 6061 passes the stress check, the premium buys nothing. Where thinning is possible, specific strength dominates and 7075 wins.

sections.heading: 7075 vs 6061 for CNC Machining
sections.text: 7075 vs 6061 for CNC Machining For most CNC-machined aluminum parts , 6061-T6 is the more economical starting point, while 7075-T6 is worth considering when the design requires higher yield strength without a major increase in part weight.

sections.heading: Cutting Performance and Tool Wear
sections.text: Cutting Performance and Tool Wear On the machine, the difference shows up in the chips before anywhere else. 6061-T6 curls into long strings and tends to weld itself onto the cutting edge at conservative speeds, which sharp polished carbide and generous lubrication keep under control, while 7075-T6 breaks into short C-shaped chips, gives a better as-machined surface, and pushes cutting forces and flank wear up at the same time. The net effect on cost between the two is small and part-specific. Both alloys run happily on carbide at 300 to 600 m/min surface speed on a modern VMC.

sections.heading: Machining Distortion and Dimensional Stability
sections.text: Machining Distortion and Dimensional Stability Residual stress in the stock is the hidden cost of cutting. When a deep pocket goes into one face of 40 mm plate and the opposite face stays solid, the remaining material rebalances and the part bows, and pocketed plates machined in a single pass commonly move a few tenths of a millimeter before anyone touches a straightedge. T651 plate, stretched at the mill, drops that risk a long way without eliminating it. Sequencing handles the rest. Rough everything first and leave 0.3 to 0.5 mm of stock; a rest period or a stress-relief cycle before the finishing cuts then keeps critical faces close to where the program put them. Support tabs left on thin sections until the late operations help as well.

sections.heading: Thin Walls, Surface Finish, and Tolerances
sections.text: Thin Walls, Surface Finish, and Tolerances Thin walls deflect under cutting force and spring back once the tool clears, in either alloy, since their elastic moduli are similar. Wall thickness and unsupported span determine the extent of deflection, while tool engagement affects the final dimensional accuracy. JLCCNC can machine metal walls as thin as 0.8 mm and plastic walls as thin as 1.5 mm. For these features, temporary ribs or tabbed stock can provide additional support and help control deformation during machining. JLCCNC applies ISO 2768-m as its default general machining tolerance. A tolerance of ±0.02 mm can be specified for individual features on the drawing, subject to a feasibility review before production. Thermal expansion also matters during inspection: both alloys have a coefficient of thermal expansion of approximately 23.5 μm/(m·K). A 100 mm part changes in length by about 23.5 μm over a 10 °C temperature difference. Parts should be allowed to stabilize at the inspection temperature before critical dimensions are measured.

sections.heading: Welding and Joining: 6061 vs 7075
sections.text: Welding and Joining: 6061 vs 7075 6061 is a weldable alloy. Standard TIG or MIG welding with ER4043 or ER5356 filler can produce sound 6061 joints. However, the heat-affected zone loses a substantial amount of its T6 strength due to overaging. Its post-weld strength depends on the welding procedure and any subsequent heat treatment, which can also introduce distortion into the assembly. Conventional fusion welding is generally not recommended for 7075 because its alloy composition makes the fusion zone highly susceptible to hot cracking. Mechanical fasteners and adhesive bonding are more practical joining methods for most machined 7075 parts. Friction stir welding is a specialized solid-state process used in some industrial and aerospace applications. The design consequence follows directly from that constraint. A simple assembly of plates and profiles is often cheaper as welded 6061, accepting the weld distortion and the softened HAZ, while a component whose loads justify 7075 usually gets machined from billet in one piece, which keeps full parent strength and holds tight feature-to-feature relationships at the cost of chip volume and cycle time. sections.heading: Is 6061 or 7075 More Cost-Effective to Machine?
sections.text: Is 6061 or 7075 More Cost-Effective to Machine? Between the two alloys, the machining cost itself barely moves, since cycle time and removal volume set the quote, with setup count close behind. 7075 wears tools somewhat faster in deep features and cuts slightly slower, against which its clean chip breaking saves finishing time, and on balance the difference is small enough to decide part by part.

sections.heading: 6061 vs 7075: Corrosion Resistance and Anodizing
sections.text: 6061 vs 7075: Corrosion Resistance and Anodizing

sections.heading: Corrosion Resistance in Different Environments
sections.text: Corrosion Resistance in Different Environments 6061 generally offers better corrosion resistance than 7075 and is often the better starting point for parts exposed to saltwater or de-icing salts. In chloride environments, 7075-T6 and 7075-T651 can develop stress corrosion cracking under sustained tensile stress. Overaged tempers such as 7075-T73 and 7075-T7351 can improve resistance to stress corrosion cracking at the cost of some strength. Neither alloy should be chosen for chemical service from a rating table, because compatibility depends on concentration and temperature as much as on the medium itself.

sections.heading: Anodizing 6061 vs 7075
sections.text: Anodizing 6061 vs 7075 Both alloys anodize, and Type II decorative coatings and Type III hard coats both work. What differs is appearance, since 6061 takes a clear, consistent film that dyes evenly across batches, while 7075's alloying elements tint the oxide gray-yellow and shift between lots, which makes color matching on mixed batches difficult. Type III hard anodizing on 7075, typically 25 to 80 μm, is the usual treatment where wear resistance matters. Anodizing changes the final dimensions of a part. As a general estimate, about half of the coating thickness may build outward from the original surface. A 15 μm Type II coating can therefore add roughly 7.5 μm to each coated surface, which may affect a close-fitting assembly or threaded feature. Specify any threads or precision mating surfaces that require protection from coating buildup, and confirm masking feasibility before production. A finish sample is also useful when color consistency is critical.

sections.heading: What Are 6061 and 7075 Aluminum Used For?
sections.text: What Are 6061 and 7075 Aluminum Used For?

sections.heading: Applications of 6061 Aluminum
sections.text: Applications of 6061 Aluminum Typical 6061 work passing through the shop includes equipment housings, mounting brackets, frames, and heat sinks. For heat sinks the 167 W/(m·K) conductivity does the work, and 6061 also carries a higher long-term service temperature, around 150 °C, before overaging becomes an issue, while 7075-T6 starts losing strength above roughly 120 °C given time. Welded assemblies and outdoor hardware round out the list, and a standard case is a machined enclosure with tapped holes and internal pockets at moderate load, anodized, delivered in 6061-T6.

sections.heading: Applications of 7075 Aluminum
sections.text: Applications of 7075 Aluminum Most of the 7075 we quote is high-load brackets and links in cycling service, plus one-piece parts that replace welded assemblies where a smaller section is worth the material premium. A drone arm is the standard example, with a small section carrying real loads while every gram is counted. Calling the alloy aerospace-grade describes the material rather than the part. Flight-qualified hardware requires material certification and traceability, which ordering 7075 stock does not provide.

sections.heading: 7075 vs 6061: Cost Comparison
sections.text: 7075 vs 6061: Cost Comparison

sections.heading: Raw Material Cost
sections.text: Raw Material Cost 6061 stock typically prices 20 to 30% under 7075, with the exact gap depending on form and lot size. Availability matters at least as much day to day, since 6061 is stocked in the widest range of sizes and ships fastest, while 7075 covers common dimensions off the shelf and odd sizes can require custom sourcing, so it is worth confirming availability before the design freezes rather than after.

sections.heading: Total CNC Part Cost
sections.text: Total CNC Part Cost A part price is not the alloy price multiplied by weight. Removal volume comes first, because machining an 8 kg housing out of a 70 kg block means paying for 62 kg of material in order to haul it away as chips, and at 7075 pricing that line item dominates the quote. Cycle time across the setups follows, and inspection load behind it wherever the tolerance scheme is tight. On small parts the alloy premium barely registers. Both alloys are fully recyclable and chips carry credit against the job, which softens the arithmetic without changing it. Whether 7075 pays is a design question with two honest answers. If the part fails, or shrinks meaningfully, because of the higher strength, the premium earns itself back, and if 6061 clears the stress check with margin, the premium buys nothing. The premium also lands unevenly on the quote, which is worth spelling out: on a part where stock accounts for 30% of the price, a 25% alloy premium moves the total by under 8%, while on heavy-removal work where the billet dominates the quote, the same premium moves it several times that. For a specific part, the material cost difference is easier to judge from the actual design. Up...

sections.heading: How to Choose Between 6061 and 7075 for CNC Parts
sections.text: How to Choose Between 6061 and 7075 for CNC Parts The selection runs in a fixed order on our side. Loads and allowable stress come first, then a decision on whether strength or stiffness governs the design, remembering that stiffness answers to geometry rather than to alloy. Corrosion exposure and finish requirements come next, and cost comes last, compared on total part cost rather than per kilogram. A drawing whose worst stress sits comfortably under 6061's yield does not improve in 7075. Drawings with thin walls and deep cavities, especially with tight positional tolerances on top of either, should come to us before release, since we review manufacturability and quote both alloys so the choice gets made on numbers instead of on property tables. sections.heading: FAQs About 7075 and 6061 Aluminum
sections.text: FAQs About 7075 and 6061 Aluminum Is 7075 aluminum stronger than 6061? Yes. 7075-T6 generally has higher tensile and yield strength than 6061-T6. The exact difference depends on the product form, thickness, and specification. Can 7075 aluminum be welded? Not by conventional fusion welding. Hot cracking in the Zn-Cu chemistry makes the joint unreliable, and the heat-affected zone loses the temper regardless. Bolted or bonded joints, or machining the part in one piece, are the workarounds. Designs that must be welded should specify 6061. Is 6061 or 7075 better for CNC machining? Both cut well. 6061 strings and builds up on edges at low speed, while 7075 breaks chips cleanly and finishes better but wears tools faster. The choice should follow the part's requirements rather than how either alloy machines. Can 6061 and 7075 aluminum both be anodized? Yes, both Type II and Type III. 6061 takes a clear, consistent film; 7075 anodizes gray-yellow with lot-to-lot variation. Cosmetic parts are safer in 6061.
